title: First Light · The Door in the Tree

speakers.name: Moss
speakers.style: A warm, low woodland storyteller. Patient, curious speech, natural pauses, quiet humour. Keep the same grounded voice throughout.

speakers.name: Wren

speakers.design_prompt: A small, bold traveller collecting stories for the dawn. Light and alert, with warmth and a sense of discovery. This direction uses a prebuilt voice; no custom voice has been created.
speakers.pronunciation_notes: Pronounce Moss as moss. Speak the dialogue exactly; do not read speaker names or directions.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Good morning, wherever the morning finds you. The mist has caught on every blade of grass. I am Moss, and beside me is Wren, who has already asked three questions before breakfast.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Four. You did not answer the one about breakfast. But yesterday, near the old oak, I found a little door. It had a brass handle shaped like a leaf.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: That oak has stood here longer than the road. Many people pass it, but almost nobody notices a door. What were you doing just before you saw it?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I had lost my way. I was following the stream, but then I followed a butterfly instead. When it disappeared, I sat down and admitted that I did not know where I was.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Ah. That is often when a door appears. Not because the forest has changed, but because we have stopped insisting that we already understand it. Was there anything written above the handle?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: There was a sentence scratched into the bark. Bring something you can give away and still keep. I tried a pine cone, then a very impressive stone. The handle did not move.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: An impressive stone is difficult to part with. But the door was asking for another kind of gift. Something that becomes larger when it is shared.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I thought it meant a song. I remembered one about a fisherman who lost his hat, but I could not remember whether he found the hat or married it.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Either ending has its possibilities. A song would have been a fine gift. So would a question or a story. What did you finally offer?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I told the door about the first time I saw the sea. The noise, the salt, and how I thought the horizon was a wall. I had been afraid to walk closer.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: And while you told that story, did it become less yours? Was it like pouring a memory into another cup and leaving your own cup empty?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: No. I remembered more. The cold sand between my toes. A woman laughing because I had brought a spoon to collect the water. By the end, I was laughing too.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Then you had found the right gift. Some things are used up when we give them. Others find their shape in the giving. A memory can sit quietly for years, waiting for somebody to listen.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: The handle turned. Inside was a round room with a table, two chairs, and a window. That bothered me. There was no window outside the tree. I checked twice.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: The oldest rooms seldom trouble themselves with sensible windows. What could you see? A garden? A hill? The place where you had first met the sea?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: A kitchen, with a kettle beginning to steam. Someone was alone at the table. I could not see their face, but they looked as though they had been waiting a long time.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Perhaps they were waiting for a story. We do not always know who needs the things we have carried. Sometimes the forest provides a door. More often, we must provide the invitation ourselves.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I told the story again, including the spoon. The person in the kitchen lifted their head and laughed. The window grew bright. When I blinked, I was outside beside the stream.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Where you had meant to go. That is a useful journey: to become lost, discover something worth sharing, and return with a better understanding of the path.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I went back this morning. No handle, no writing, no door. But somebody had left a little spoon between the roots. Did the story reach the right person?

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: I think we should be careful about calling any kitchen ordinary. Keep the spoon, not as proof that the door was real, but as a reminder to notice who is listening.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Then here is a question for anyone listening now. What is one small memory you could give away today? It need not have a sea in it. A familiar voice, an unexpected kindness, or a breakfast might be enough.

turns.speaker: Moss
turns.text: Carry that question gently. There is no hurry to answer. The morning is still unfolding, and somewhere a kettle is beginning to sing. Thank you for spending these few minutes with us at First Light.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I am Wren, still curious and finally ready for breakfast. And I am taking the spoon. Until next time, leave a little room for stories you have not heard.
